alg-01.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: An algorithm is a step-by-step way of solving a problem. Your mentor gave you “Grokking Algorithms” and LeetCode for a reason: algorithmic problems are the filter at interviews, and on the job they decide whether a Data Engineer's table is processed in a second or in an hour.
alg-01.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: This track is a summary of the book's key chapters plus exercises. Read the book alongside it (the PDF is in your mentor folder): here you get the essence and the practice, there the pictures and the details.
alg-01.lessons.0.title: Why you need algorithms
alg-01.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Big O notation answers one question: “how much longer will this run if the data grows ten times?”
alg-01.lessons.1.blocks.1.html:
• O(1) — instant, independent of size (fetching a list element by index)
  • O(log n) — almost instant (binary search)
  • O(n) — proportional to the data (a loop over a list)
  • O(n²) — squared: ten times the data → a hundred times longer (a loop inside a loop)
alg-01.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: A million elements: logarithmic — 20 steps, linear — a million, quadratic — a trillion. This is why the choice of algorithm matters more than the speed of the computer.
alg-01.lessons.1.title: Big-O: rate of growth
alg-01.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: The simplest search: walk the list until you find it. In the worst case you look at everything:
alg-01.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: Returning the index or -1 is the standard convention. For unsorted data nothing beats a linear search.
alg-01.lessons.2.title: Linear search — O(n)
alg-01.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: If the list is sorted, you can search far more cleverly: look at the middle and immediately throw away half. Like guessing a number: “higher or lower than 50?”
alg-01.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: The two pointers low and high halve the search area at every step. A billion elements — 30 steps at most!
alg-01.lessons.3.title: Binary search — O(log n)
alg-01.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: Binary search works only on sorted data. On an unsorted list it silently returns nonsense:
alg-01.lessons.4.blocks.1.html:
• The data is already sorted → binary search, O(log n)
  • Unsorted, searching once → linear, O(n)
  • Unsorted, searching many times → sort first (or use a dictionary — that comes in module 4)
alg-01.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: This reasoning — “what pays off once you count the preparation” — is engineering thinking itself. It is tested at every interview.
alg-01.lessons.4.title: The main pitfall
alg-01.quiz.0.explain: Big O is about the rate of GROWTH of operations, not about seconds.
alg-01.quiz.0.options.1: How the number of operations grows as the data grows
alg-01.quiz.0.options.3: The number of lines of code
alg-01.quiz.0.q: What does Big O notation show?
alg-01.quiz.1.explain: Access by index is constant: it does not depend on the list's length.
alg-01.quiz.2.explain: Every step discards half — a logarithm.
alg-01.quiz.3.q: The maximum number of binary-search steps in a list of 128 elements?
alg-01.quiz.4.explain: Without sorting, “discard half” does not work — the result would be wrong.
alg-01.quiz.4.q: The essential precondition of binary search?
alg-01.quiz.5.explain: n iterations of the outer × n of the inner = n² operations.
alg-01.quiz.5.q: A loop inside a loop over one list is usually…
alg-01.tagline: Big-O and your first real algorithm · Grokking ch. 1
alg-01.tasks.0.desc: Write a function linear_search(items, target): return the index of the first occurrence of target in the list, or -1 if it is absent. The .index() method is not allowed — use a loop!
alg-01.tasks.0.hint: for i in range(len(items)): if items[i] == target: return i. After the loop, return -1.
alg-01.tasks.0.title: Linear search
alg-01.tasks.1.desc: Write a function binary_search(items, target) for a sorted list: return the element's index or -1. Use the two pointers low/high as in the theory.
alg-01.tasks.1.hint: mid = (low + high) // 2. If items[mid] < target then low = mid + 1; if greater, high = mid - 1.
alg-01.tasks.1.title: Binary search
alg-01.tasks.2.desc: Write a function binary_steps(items, target) — the same binary search, but it returns the number of midpoint checks it took to find the element (or -1 if the element is absent).
alg-01.tasks.2.hint: Put steps += 1 right inside the while, before the comparison. On a hit return steps; after the loop return -1.
alg-01.tasks.2.title: How many steps?
alg-01.title: Complexity and binary search

alg-02.exam.questions.1.options.1: Adjacent elements that are in the wrong order

alg-02.exam.tasks.0.desc: Write a function sort_desc(items) that returns a new list in descending order, using your own algorithm (selection or bubble), without sorted() or .sort().
alg-02.exam.tasks.0.title: Sort descending
alg-02.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Sorting is foundational: binary search, reports, top-10 lists, de-duplication — everything starts with “sort it first”. Python has a built-in sort, but interviews ask you to write your own, to check whether you understand what happens under the hood.
alg-02.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: key= is the superpower of the built-in sort: sort by any attribute you like. Remember it for Pandas later.
alg-02.lessons.0.title: The sorting problem
alg-02.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Selection sort from the book: find the minimum → move it to the result → repeat with what is left.
alg-02.lessons.1.blocks.1.html:
• Step 1: in [29, 5, 71, 34] the minimum is 5 → result [5]
  • Step 2: in [29, 71, 34] the minimum is 29 → [5, 29]
  • Step 3: in [71, 34] the minimum is 34 → [5, 29, 34]
  • Step 4: [5, 29, 34, 71] — done
alg-02.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Each search for a minimum is O(n) and we repeat it n times → O(n²) in total. Unacceptable for a million rows, ideal for learning.
alg-02.lessons.1.title: Selection sort — the idea
alg-02.lessons.2.blocks.1.html: Splitting into two functions is good style: find_smallest_index searches, selection_sort orchestrates. Exactly as in the book.
alg-02.lessons.2.title: Selection sort — the code
alg-02.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: Bubble sort is the second teaching algorithm: walk the list and swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. Large values “bubble up” to the end:
alg-02.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: Note the swap: a, b = b, a — the Pythonic way to exchange values without a temporary variable. Also O(n²).
alg-02.lessons.3.title: Bubble sort
alg-02.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: Quicksort (chapter 4 of the book) and its relatives run in O(n·log n) — an enormous difference:
alg-02.lessons.4.blocks.1.html: • n = 1,000,000: n² is a trillion operations, n·log n is about 20 million — 50,000 times faster
alg-02.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: Python's built-in sorted() is Timsort, O(n·log n). The engineer's rule: in production use sorted(); in study and at interviews be able to write selection/bubble yourself and explain their complexity.
alg-02.lessons.4.title: What is used in the real world
alg-02.quiz.0.explain: We search for a minimum n times at O(n) each — O(n²) in total.
alg-02.quiz.1.explain: key defines what to sort by — here the length of the string.
alg-02.quiz.2.explain: Selection = “select the minimum of what remains”, repeated n times.
alg-02.quiz.2.options.1: Repeatedly find the minimum and move it to the result
alg-02.quiz.3.explain: The Pythonic value swap — the basis of bubble sort.
alg-02.quiz.3.options.1: Swaps the values of the variables
alg-02.quiz.3.q: What does a, b = b, a do?
alg-02.quiz.4.explain: Timsort — O(n·log n), which is why we use it in real code.
alg-02.quiz.4.q: The complexity of the built-in sorted()?
alg-02.quiz.5.q: How do you sort from large to small with the built-in?
alg-02.tagline: Selection and bubble sort · Grokking ch. 2
alg-02.tasks.0.desc: Write a function find_smallest_index(items) — return the index of the smallest element. No min() and no .index() — a loop only!
alg-02.tasks.0.hint: for i in range(1, len(items)): if items[i] < items[smallest]: smallest = i. Return smallest at the end.
alg-02.tasks.0.title: Index of the minimum
alg-02.tasks.1.desc: Write a function selection_sort(items) that returns a NEW sorted list (ascending). Use your own minimum-finding logic. sorted() and .sort() are forbidden!
alg-02.tasks.1.hint: while src: idx = index of the minimum of src; result.append(src.pop(idx)). Return result.
alg-02.tasks.1.title: Selection sort
alg-02.tasks.2.desc: You are given a list of (name, score) tuples. Write a function top_students(students) that returns a list of names sorted by score from highest to lowest. Here you may (and should!) use sorted() with key.
alg-02.tasks.2.hint: ordered = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True), then collect the names: [s[0] for s in ordered] or with a loop.
alg-02.tasks.2.title: Top students

alg-03.exam.questions.0.options.1: A base case and a recursive case
alg-03.exam.questions.0.q: The two mandatory parts of a recursion?
alg-03.exam.questions.2.options.0: There is a bug in the base case
alg-03.exam.questions.4.q: Recursion versus a loop — what does the book say?
alg-03.exam.tasks.0.desc: Write a recursive function fib(n): fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, and beyond that fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). The legendary interview problem!
alg-03.exam.tasks.0.title: Fibonacci numbers
alg-03.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: Recursion is when a function calls itself with a “smaller” version of the problem. A countdown, recursively:
alg-03.lessons.0.blocks.2.html:
Every recursion has two parts:

  • The base case — when to stop (without it you get infinity and a crash)
  • The recursive case — calling itself with a smaller problem
alg-03.lessons.0.title: A function calling itself
alg-03.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: Every function call is placed on the stack — a pile of “unfinished business”. Recursion grows the pile and then unwinds it from the top:
alg-03.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: See the “staircase”? The calls go deeper until the base case, then the results come back up. The stack is not infinite: too deep a recursion gives a RecursionError.
alg-03.lessons.1.title: The call stack
alg-03.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: Summing a list recursively (an example straight from the book): the sum is the first element plus the sum of the rest:
alg-03.lessons.2.title: Classics: factorial and sum
alg-03.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: Anything you can do with recursion you can do with a loop, and vice versa. A loop is usually faster and safer (no stack overflow). Recursion wins where the problem is nested by nature:
alg-03.lessons.3.blocks.1.html:
• Walking folders with subfolders (a file system is a tree)
  • Nested JSON (data inside data — a Data Engineer's constant task!)
  • Quicksort, walking trees and graphs
alg-03.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: A quote from the book: “recursion gives no gain in speed — it gives clarity”. Choose whichever is clearer to whoever reads the code.
alg-03.lessons.3.title: When recursion, when a loop
alg-03.quiz.0.explain: With no stop condition the function calls itself forever until the call stack bursts.
alg-03.quiz.0.q: What happens to a recursion with no base case?
alg-03.quiz.1.explain: The factorial of 1 (and 0) is 1 — that is where the recursion stops.
alg-03.quiz.2.explain: Every call is placed on top and every finished one is removed. Recursion uses it heavily.
alg-03.quiz.2.options.1: A pile of unfinished function calls
alg-03.quiz.3.explain: An empty list is the base case and returns 0.
alg-03.quiz.3.q: What does rec_sum([]) from the theory return?
alg-03.quiz.4.explain: Nested structures are “recursive themselves” — the code becomes natural and short.
alg-03.quiz.4.options.1: For nested structures: trees, folders, JSON
alg-03.tagline: Base and recursive cases, the call stack · Grokking ch. 3
alg-03.tasks.0.desc: Write a recursive function factorial(n). Loops are forbidden — recursion only!
alg-03.tasks.0.hint: if n <= 1: return 1. Otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
alg-03.tasks.0.title: Factorial
alg-03.tasks.1.desc: Write a recursive function rec_sum(items) — the sum of a list of numbers. No sum() and no loops: the first element plus the recursive sum of the rest (items[1:]).
alg-03.tasks.1.hint: if not items: return 0. Otherwise return items[0] + rec_sum(items[1:]).
alg-03.tasks.1.title: Recursive sum
alg-03.tasks.2.desc: Write a recursive function power(a, n) — raise a to the whole power n (n ≥ 0). The ** operator and pow() are forbidden: a^n = a · a^(n-1), base a^0 = 1.
alg-03.tasks.2.hint: if n == 0: return 1. Otherwise return a * power(a, n - 1).
alg-03.tasks.2.title: Power of a number
alg-03.title: Recursion

alg-04.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: You already use hash tables — that is Python's dict! A hash function turns a key into a slot number, so lookup by key is O(1), instant at any size.
alg-04.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: Compare: searching a list is O(n), a sorted list O(log n), a dictionary O(1). That is why “could a dictionary help here?” is the first question when optimising.
alg-04.lessons.0.title: Hash tables — the most useful tool
alg-04.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: 1) Lookups — a phone book, DNS, settings. 2) Duplicate checks — “has this person already voted?”. 3) Caching — remember a result so you need not compute it again:
alg-04.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Collisions (two keys in one slot) do happen, but a good hash function makes them rare — on average it stays O(1). Answer exactly that at an interview.
alg-04.lessons.1.title: Three uses from the book
alg-04.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: A graph is vertices (nodes) connected by edges. It models everything connected: friends in a social network, roads between cities, task dependencies in Airflow (a DAG is a graph!).
alg-04.lessons.2.blocks.1.html: In Python a graph is conveniently stored as a dictionary “vertex → list of neighbours”:
alg-04.lessons.2.title: Graphs — nodes and edges
alg-04.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: BFS (breadth-first search) walks a graph in “waves”: first the neighbours, then their neighbours. It answers “is there a path?” and “which path is shortest?” (by number of steps):
alg-04.lessons.3.blocks.2.html: Two key pieces: a queue (deque — take from the front, add to the back) and visited (do not walk in circles). Learn this template — it solves dozens of LeetCode problems.
alg-04.lessons.3.title: BFS — breadth-first search
alg-04.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: After this module you have the whole starter kit: complexity, search, sorting, recursion, hash tables, BFS. The mentor's plan calls for 50+ problems. Start like this:
alg-04.lessons.4.blocks.1.html:
• LeetCode → Problems → difficulty Easy → topics Array, Hash Table, Two Pointers
  • Begin with the legends: Two Sum, Valid Palindrome, Merge Sorted Array, Contains Duplicate
  • Think for 15–30 minutes yourself → look at other people's solutions → understand them → solve it again on your own
  • Push what you solved to GitHub with comments — as the mentor asked
alg-04.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: Your baptism by fire — the Two Sum problem (number 1 on LeetCode) — awaits you in this module's exam. 😉
alg-04.lessons.4.title: You are ready for LeetCode
